title: One Church, twenty-four churches
hookLine: the Latin Church and the Eastern Catholic churches, all in communion with Rome

cards: A few streets from a parish with pews and a kneeler in every row, there's another church. Golden domes. Inside, a wall of icons, a cloud of incense, a priest with a beard, candles burning in front of the icons.

The bulletin is in English and Ukrainian. A Catholic from the first parish walks in, a little unsure, and asks the woman at the door whether this is an Orthodox church. She smiles; she gets asked that a lot.
No, she says. We're Catholic. We just aren't Roman.

teach.h: SUI IURIS: OF ITS OWN LAW.
teach.b: You met one of these churches, the Ukrainian Greek Catholics, earlier on this path. First, the phrase. Sui iuris is Latin for of its own law.

The Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches uses it for a church with its own hierarchy, recognized as self-governing by the Church's highest authority: its own bishops, sometimes its own patriarch, its own law, liturgy, calendar, saints and ways of praying.
And all of it in full communion with the bishop of Rome. Second, the families.
The Catechism names the great liturgical traditions in the Church: the Latin, and then the Byzantine, the Alexandrian or Coptic, the Syriac, the Armenian, the Maronite and the Chaldean.
Out of them come the Eastern Catholic churches: Ukrainians and Melkites, Maronites in Lebanon, Syro-Malabar Catholics in India, Chaldeans from Iraq, Copts, Ethiopians, Armenians and more.
Third, equal dignity. The Second Vatican Council, in its decree on the Eastern churches, said these churches are of equal dignity, and that none outranks another because of its rite.

The Latin Church sits at that table as one church among them, not the owner of the house. The Council asked the Eastern churches to keep their own traditions whole, not trade them for Latin ones. Fourth, the picture.
Pope John Paul the Second wrote that the Church must breathe with both its lungs, East and West. Catholic doesn't only mean Roman.
For a Latin Catholic, the parish with the domes isn't a stranger's church. It belongs to the same communion.

how: Eastern Catholics belong to their own churches sui iuris, with their own bishops, liturgy and law, while in full communion with the pope; Latin Catholics may attend their liturgies, and in some cities Eastern Catholic parishes stand a few streets from Latin ones.

p: no church outranks another by rite

games.q: you lead an Eastern church in full communion with Rome. what does the Council ask you to do with your own liturgy and customs?
o: replace them with the Latin ones.
keep them whole, and return to them where they've been lost.
keep the liturgy but give up your own law.
games.why: the decree on the Eastern churches asks them to keep their own rites and way of life, as churches of equal dignity.

practice: Picture your town or city from above: somewhere in it, or not far off, there may be a church whose people pray in Arabic, Ukrainian, Malayalam or Syriac, and who are Catholic too.
You don't need to know where; just hold them as part of the same family. If you pray, pray for them in any words you know; if not, simply let the map grow larger than it was this morning.

wordCard.voice: Sui iuris. Of its own law: a church with its own hierarchy, liturgy and law, in full communion with Rome. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: of its own law, or in its own right.

carryVoice: Your line: one church, many churches. Each with its own law, all in one communion. Go gently.
